messages.subject: R/qtl version 1.11-12
messages.body_plain:
A new version of R/qtl (1.11-12) has been released at its web site
(http://www.rqtl.org).

See http://www.rqtl.org/STATUS.txt for a list of changes.  There was
just one major change (see below).

Another important announcement: Saunak Sen and I have just completed a
book, "A guide to QTL mapping with R/qtl", which will be published by
Springer and will appear in early August.  See http://www.rqtl.org/book
for further details (including the table of contents and a sample
chapter).

Karl Broman
kbr...@biostat.wisc.edu

------

Version 1.11, 3/29/2009:

Major changes:

  Revised effectplot so that one may refer to "pseudomarkers" by their
  chromosome and position with a construction like "5...@32.8", rather
  than having to first call find.pseudomarker to get the name.  Also,
  in the actual plot, we use the form "5...@32.8" rather than, for
  example, "c5.loc47".

messages.subject: How many QTL we need?
messages.body_plain:
Dear all:

I'm the master degree student from National Taiwan University.

my teacher and i are both working on analysing my experimental data.

my experiment is to study the QTL of rice with 286 individuals and 147
markers.

now, we got a little problem about how many QTL we need?

when we use stepwiseqtl function, we might find around 10 QTL and with
interaction between some of them.

but according to Darvasi's (1997) paper when the proportion of
variance explained is less than 5% the confidance interval is more
than 50cM, almost half of the chromosome in rice.

so, if we use stepwise method to detect QTL but the R^2 of the QTL is
less than 5%, should we thak them in to acount?

or when should we stop detecting QTL?

reference
Darvasi A. (1997) A simple Method to Calculate Resolving Power and
Confidence Interval of QTL Map Location. Behavior Genetics Vol 27, No.
2. p.125

messages.subject: Re: [Rqtl-disc] How many QTL we need?
messages.body_plain:
I'm surprised that you are able to find so many QTL, and that you are
able to map QTL that are responsible for <5% of the phenotypic
variance, with just 286 individuals.

The size of the QTL interval should depend not just on the percent
phenotypic variance explained by the QTL but also by the size of the
cross, and by the chance location of crossovers in your particular
cross.

I would focus on the conditional LOD scores of the QTL, in considering
whether they are trustworthy or not, rather than on the percent
variance explained.

In your use of the stepwiseqtl function, did you use a permutation
test with scantwo, followed by calc.penalties to get the penalties, or
did you use the default penalties (which were based on simulations for
the mouse genome)?

Regards,
karl
-----------
Karl Broman
kbr...@biostat.wisc.edu
http://www.biostat.wisc.edu/~kbroman
